claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings resist time-dependent plastic deformation.
Numerous chemically disordered interfaces act as robust barriers to dislocation motion.
Interface-mediated barriers delay plastic flow relative to homogeneous alloys.
The proposed initial material is an as-deposited, crystalline HEA multilayer coating with distinct compositionally complex interfaces.
The coating should be subjected to sustained mechanical load for an extended period at a controlled temperature below the onset of significant thermal diffusion.
Multilayer HEA coatings should be compared under identical test conditions with homogeneous HEA films or conventional alloys lacking well-defined multilayer interfaces.
Keeping the temperature sufficiently low prevents interface deterioration during testing.
Distinct, chemically disordered multilayer interfaces effectively pin dislocations.
Chemical complexity at multilayer interfaces disrupts dislocation nucleation.
Chemical complexity at multilayer interfaces disrupts dislocation propagation.
Interfacial barriers delay the dislocation motion and accumulation that would otherwise produce time-dependent plastic deformation.
Under constant load, multilayer HEA coatings will exhibit a slower strain rate than baseline homogeneous coatings.
Under constant load, multilayer HEA coatings will retain higher yield strength over time than baseline homogeneous coatings.
In-situ observations will show significant dislocation pile-up at multilayer interfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies only when loading and temperature do not cause significant interface degradation, rapid diffusion, or phase changes.
Testing must last long enough for time-dependent plasticity to manifest, potentially for durations up to 1000 hours.
Residual stress or grain-boundary strengthening independent of interface dislocation pinning may alternatively explain resistance to plastic deformation.

Failure to observe slower strain rates or higher yield strength in multilayer coatings, or failure to observe preferential interfacial dislocation accumulation, would falsify the proposed interface-pinning mechanism.
